title: REST API design (resources, status codes, errors)
scopeHtml: Scope: REST principles, resource and URL design, HTTP methods and idempotency, status codes, error format, payload design, security basics, async operations.

notes.title: What REST really is
notes.html:
REST is a style for building web APIs around "things" (resources) that you name with URLs and act on with a small fixed set of verbs (HTTP methods). The URL says what, the method says what to do, the status code says how it went.

A resource is a noun: a user, an order, a photo. /orders/42 is order number 42. You do not invent verbs in the URL (/getOrder, /deleteUser); HTTP already gives you GET and DELETE.

The core ideas (Roy Fielding's thesis, 2000):

  • Client-server: the two sides evolve independently.
  • Stateless: every request carries everything the server needs (auth token, ids). The server keeps no per-client conversation in memory, so any instance can serve any request.
  • Uniform interface: same verbs, same URL patterns everywhere.
  • Cacheable: responses say whether they may be cached.
  • Representations: the server sends JSON (or XML), not the database row itself.

Worked example. Swiggy-style app: GET /restaurants/17/menu returns the menu, POST /orders creates an order, GET /orders/9001 reads it. 3 calls, 3 nouns, zero verbs in URLs.

Industry examples. Stripe's API is the classic "good REST": /v1/charges, /v1/customers/{id}, consistent errors. GitHub's REST API uses /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues. Most real "REST" APIs are really "JSON over HTTP"; pure HATEOAS (links that drive the client) is rare.

Everyday analogy. A library: every book has a shelf address (URL). The few things you can do are borrow, return, look (verbs). You never invent a new kind of action per book.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying REST means "JSON over HTTP". Statelessness and the uniform interface are the point.
  • Putting verbs in URLs and calling it REST.
  • Forgetting that stateless does not mean "no database"; it means no per-client memory on the server.

notes.title: Resource naming and URL design
notes.html:
Use plural nouns, hierarchy for ownership, and query params for filters.

Do Don't
GET /users/7/orders GET /getUserOrders?id=7
POST /orders POST /createOrder
GET /orders?status=PAID&limit=20 GET /orders/paid/20
DELETE /carts/3/items/55 POST /removeItem

Rules of thumb:

  • Collection /orders, single item /orders/{id}.
  • Nest at most 2 levels (/users/7/orders/42). Deeper nests are brittle; once an order has a global id, /orders/42 is enough.
  • Lowercase, hyphens (/order-items), no trailing slash, no file extensions.
  • For actions that are not CRUD, model the action as a resource: POST /orders/42/cancellation or POST /payments/99/refunds (creates a refund). Pragmatic escape hatch: POST /orders/42:cancel (Google style). Pick one style and keep it.
  • Use opaque, non-guessable ids (UUID/ULID) if enumeration is a risk; sequential ids leak your volume ("we have 1.2M orders").

Decision gravity. URL shapes are a one-way door once public clients (mobile apps you cannot force to update) depend on them. An Android app version from 2 years ago still calls your old URL. Changing it means versioning (see the versioning note). Choose carefully before launch.

Industry examples. Stripe: POST /v1/payment_intents/{id}/confirm (action as sub-path). Google APIs: POST /v1/projects/x/instances/y:start. Twitter/X v2: GET /2/users/:id/tweets.

Everyday analogy. A postal address: country, city, street, house. Hierarchy reads left to right and each part narrows it down.

Common interview traps.

  • Deep nesting like /a/1/b/2/c/3/d/4.
  • Using GET with a body or for anything that changes state (crawlers and prefetchers will trigger it).
  • Mixing singular and plural (/user/7, /orders).

notes.title: HTTP methods: safe, idempotent, and what they mean
notes.html:
Safe = does not change server state. Idempotent = doing it N times has the same effect as doing it once.

Method Use Safe Idempotent Body
GET Read yes yes no
HEAD Headers only yes yes no
POST Create / action no no yes
PUT Replace whole resource no yes yes
PATCH Partial update no not guaranteed yes
DELETE Remove no yes rarely
OPTIONS Capabilities / CORS preflight yes yes no

Why idempotency matters: networks fail. If the phone sends PUT /users/7 {name:"Asha"} and the response is lost, retrying is harmless. If it sends POST /payments and retries, you may charge twice. That is why POST needs an idempotency key (covered in the pagination/idempotency note).

PUT vs PATCH:

// PUT /users/7  replaces everything; missing fields become null/default
{ "name": "Asha", "email": "a@x.com", "city": "Pune" }

// PATCH /users/7  changes only what is sent
{ "city": "Mumbai" }

JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) is the simple PATCH; JSON Patch (RFC 6902) is an array of operations (add, remove, replace).

DELETE idempotency nuance: first call returns 204, second may return 404. The server state is the same (gone), so it is still idempotent; the response differs. Interviewers like this nuance.

Worked example. Android app on a flaky 3G connection retries on timeout (OkHttp retryOnConnectionFailure is true by default). 1% of calls retry. With 1M POST /payments a day that is up to 10,000 possible duplicate charges unless the server deduplicates.

Industry examples. Stripe requires an Idempotency-Key header for POST. AWS S3 PUT object is idempotent by design. Kubernetes uses PATCH heavily (strategic merge patch).

Everyday analogy. A light switch labelled "turn ON" (PUT) is idempotent: pressing twice leaves it on. A "toggle" switch (POST) is not: pressing twice turns it off.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying PUT and PATCH are the same.
  • Believing DELETE must return the same status each time.
  • Using POST for everything, losing caching and retry safety.

notes.title: Status codes you must know
notes.html:
The first digit tells the story: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx you (the client) made a mistake, 5xx we (the server) failed.

Code Meaning Use when
200 OK Success with body GET, PUT, PATCH result
201 Created New resource POST; include Location: /orders/42
202 Accepted Queued, not done yet Async job; return a status URL
204 No Content Success, empty body DELETE, PUT with nothing to return
301/308 Moved permanently URL change (308 keeps the method)
304 Not Modified Cache still valid Conditional GET with ETag
400 Bad Request Malformed / invalid input Bad JSON, validation failure
401 Unauthorized Not authenticated Missing/expired token
403 Forbidden Authenticated, not allowed Wrong role
404 Not Found No such resource Also used to hide existence
405 Method not allowed DELETE on a read-only URL
409 Conflict State conflict Duplicate, version mismatch
410 Gone Removed on purpose Deprecated endpoint
412 Precondition Failed If-Match mismatch Optimistic locking
415 Unsupported media type Wrong Content-Type
422 Unprocessable Content Well-formed but semantically invalid Business-rule validation
429 Too Many Requests Rate limited Send Retry-After
500 Internal Server Error Our bug Never leak stack traces
502 / 503 / 504 Bad gateway / unavailable / gateway timeout Upstream down / overloaded / slow

Why codes matter for the client: 4xx (except 408/429) should not be retried (the same request will fail the same way), 5xx and 429 may be retried with backoff. Retrying 400s hammers your server for nothing.

401 vs 403 is the most-asked confusion: 401 = "who are you?" (should carry WWW-Authenticate), 403 = "I know who you are, and no". 400 vs 422: many teams use 400 for malformed syntax and 422 for valid-syntax-but-business-invalid; either is acceptable if consistent.

Industry examples. Stripe uses 402 for card declines and 409 for idempotency conflicts. GitHub returns 404 instead of 403 for private repos you cannot see, to avoid leaking existence. Cloudflare has its own 52x codes for origin problems.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant: 2xx "here is your food", 4xx "you ordered something we do not serve", 5xx "the kitchen is on fire".

Common interview traps.

  • Returning 200 with {"error": ...} in the body. Monitoring, caches and clients all misread it.
  • Returning 500 for validation errors (pollutes error-rate alerts).
  • Using 404 for an empty list; an empty collection is 200 [].

notes.title: Error response design
notes.html:
Every error should have the same shape so one client handler works for all endpoints. The standard is RFC 7807 / RFC 9457 "Problem Details" (application/problem+json).

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/insufficient-funds",
  "title": "Insufficient funds",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Balance 120.00 is less than the 250.00 requested.",
  "instance": "/payments/abc123",
  "code": "INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS",
  "request_id": "req_8f3a1c",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "amount", "message": "must be <= balance" }
  ]
}

Design rules:

  • A stable machine-readable code (clients switch on this), a human detail (shown to users or logs). Never make clients parse the message text.
  • Include a request/trace id so support can find the exact log line.
  • Field-level errors for validation: return all of them at once, not one per round trip.
  • Never leak stack traces, SQL, internal hostnames. Log them server-side under the request id.
  • Be careful with auth errors: "wrong password" vs "no such user" enables account enumeration.

Kotlin client example (Retrofit).

data class ApiError(val code: String, val detail: String?, val request_id: String?)

fun Response<*>.toApiError(moshi: Moshi): ApiError? =
    errorBody()?.source()?.let { moshi.adapter(ApiError::class.java).fromJson(it) }

Industry examples. Stripe's error object has type, code, message, param, request_log_url. Google APIs return google.rpc.Status with code, message, details[]. Spring Boot 3 has built-in ProblemDetail support.

Everyday analogy. A hospital form: the same boxes (code, description, ticket number) for every complaint, so any nurse can process it.

Common interview traps.

  • Free-text-only errors that force clients to string-match.
  • Different error shapes from different microservices leaking through the gateway.
  • Detailed 500 bodies exposing internals (a security finding).

notes.title: Request and response design
notes.html:
Keep payloads predictable: consistent field naming, ISO dates, explicit nulls, and envelopes only when they add value.

  • Naming: pick snake_case or camelCase and never mix. Stripe uses snake_case; Google JSON uses camelCase.
  • Dates: ISO 8601 in UTC: "2026-11-09T10:15:30Z". Never send epoch millis ambiguously or local time without offset.
  • Money: integers in the smallest unit ("amount": 1999, "currency": "INR" means 19.99 rupees if 2 decimals) or decimal strings. Never floats (0.1 + 0.2 problem).
  • Big ids: send 64-bit ids as strings; JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53.
  • Enums: strings ("PAID"), and tell clients to tolerate unknown values (forward compatibility).
  • Envelope or not: bare arrays cannot grow (no room for next_cursor). Prefer {"data":[...], "next_cursor":"..."} for collections.
  • Partial responses: ?fields=id,name or ?expand=customer to cut payload size for mobile.
  • Content negotiation: Accept / Content-Type headers; Accept-Encoding: gzip cuts JSON by 70 to 90%.

Worked example. A feed item of 2 KB JSON, 20 items = 40 KB per page. gzip brings it to about 6 KB. On a 1 Mbps mobile link that is 0.32 s vs 0.05 s. With fields= trimming to 600 bytes per item, 12 KB raw, about 2.5 KB gzipped. Mobile APIs care about this.

Caching with ETag (conditional GET).

curl -i /products/5            # 200, ETag: "v17", Cache-Control: max-age=60
curl -i -H 'If-None-Match: "v17"' /products/5   # 304, no body

Optimistic locking: client sends If-Match: "v17" on PUT; if the record changed you get 412.

Industry examples. Instagram Graph API uses fields=. Shopify returns money as decimal strings. GitHub supports ETag conditional requests and does not count 304s against your rate limit.

Everyday analogy. Ordering a parcel: label format, units and packaging are agreed once, so the courier never guesses.

Common interview traps.

  • Floats for money.
  • Returning a bare top-level array, then needing pagination later (breaking change).
  • Renaming a field "because it is nicer" (breaking for old app versions).

notes.title: Security basics for REST APIs
notes.html:
Authenticate who, authorize what, and protect the transport.

  • HTTPS everywhere (TLS 1.2+). HTTP only redirects.
  • Authentication: OAuth 2.0 access tokens (short-lived, 5 to 60 min) plus refresh tokens; JWT as a signed, self-contained token, or opaque tokens looked up server-side (revocable). API keys for server-to-server.
  • Authorization: check on every request and every object. The most common real-world bug is BOLA/IDOR: GET /orders/42 works for any logged-in user because the code only checked "logged in", not "is order 42 theirs?" (OWASP API Top 10 #1).
  • Input validation at the edge: size limits (body 1 MB), types, allow-lists. Parameterized queries only.
  • CORS for browser clients: allow-list origins; never * with credentials.
  • Rate limiting and request size limits (see the rate limiting note).
  • Mass assignment: don't bind the request JSON straight onto a DB entity; a client could send "role":"admin".

Industry examples. Stripe: restricted API keys with per-resource scopes. Many 2019+ breaches (Peloton, Optus 2022 unauthenticated endpoint) were missing authorization, not broken crypto.

Everyday analogy. A hotel: the front desk checks your ID (authentication), your key card opens only your room (authorization), not every door.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting tokens in URLs (they land in logs). Use the Authorization: Bearer header.
  • JWT with no expiry or a secret hard-coded in the Android app.
  • Checking authorization only in the UI.

notes.title: Idempotency, caching and design choices at a glance
notes.html:
A good API makes the common failure (a retry) safe and the common read (a repeat GET) cheap.

Decisions you should state in an interview:

Decision Chosen Alternative Breaks when Reversible?
Style REST/JSON gRPC, GraphQL Many round trips, strict typing needed Costly (new surface)
IDs UUID/ULID Auto-increment Index locality (UUIDv4 random inserts) One-way once exposed
Money Integer minor units Decimal string Currencies with 0 or 3 decimals ignored Hard
Errors Problem Details Ad-hoc Inconsistent across teams Easy to add, hard to change
Versioning Prefix /v1 or header None Breaking change with old apps One-way door

Async operations: for work taking more than a second or two, return 202 Accepted with Location: /jobs/77; the client polls GET /jobs/77 (or receives a webhook). That avoids long-held connections and gateway timeouts (often 30 to 60 s).

Industry examples. Google Cloud long-running operations (operations/123). Stripe payment intents move through states and notify by webhook. YouTube video upload uses resumable upload sessions.

Everyday analogy. A dry-cleaner gives you a ticket (202 plus job URL). You come back and show it; you do not stand at the counter for 3 days.

Common interview traps.

  • Holding an HTTP request open for a 2-minute report and hitting the load balancer timeout.
  • Not defining what a retry of a non-idempotent call does.
  • Skipping the "who calls this and can I force them to upgrade?" question (decides how breaking you can be).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• REST = resources (nouns) + HTTP verbs + status codes, stateless, cacheable. Most real APIs are "JSON over HTTP" with REST flavour.
  • URLs: plural nouns, shallow nesting, filters in the query string; actions as sub-resources. Public URLs are a one-way door.
  • Know safe vs idempotent: GET/PUT/DELETE idempotent, POST not (needs idempotency keys), PATCH depends.
  • Status codes: 2xx ok, 4xx client error (do not retry except 429/408), 5xx server (retry with backoff). 401 = who are you, 403 = not allowed. Never 200 with an error body.
  • Errors: one stable shape (RFC 9457), machine code, human detail, request id, field errors, no internals.
  • Payloads: ISO UTC dates, money as integers, ids as strings, envelope for collections, gzip, ETag, fields= for mobile.
  • Security: HTTPS, short-lived tokens, object-level authorization on every request (BOLA), validation, no mass assignment.
  • Slow work: 202 plus a job URL, not a held-open request.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a safe and an idempotent HTTP method, and why does it matter for a mobile client?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who memorised the verb table from people who know why retries are or are not dangerous.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Safe means the call does not change server state, like GET. Idempotent means calling it N times leaves the same state as calling it once, like PUT and DELETE. Every safe method is idempotent but not the other way round. It matters because networks drop responses: I can blindly retry an idempotent call, but a POST retry can create a duplicate, so POST needs an idempotency key.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Idempotency is about server state after the call, not about the response. DELETE returns 204 first time and 404 the second time, yet state (resource gone) is identical, so it is idempotent.

Method  Safe  Idempotent
GET     yes   yes
PUT     no    yes   (replace whole resource)
DELETE  no    yes
POST    no    no    (create / action)
PATCH   no    not guaranteed ({"city":"X"} is, {"visits":"+1"} is not)

HTTP clients and proxies act on these promises: browsers prefetch GET, OkHttp retries on connection failure by default, load balancers may replay idempotent calls. If you hide a state change behind GET, a crawler or prefetcher triggers it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
curl -X PUT  /users/7 -d '{"name":"Asha","city":"Pune"}'   # retry safe
curl -X POST /payments -d '{"amount":1999}'                # retry may double charge

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying PUT and PATCH are the same; PUT replaces, PATCH changes only sent fields.
  • Believing DELETE must return the same status each time.
  • Using GET for actions like /users/7/delete.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is PATCH idempotent? -> Not guaranteed. Setting a field is; an increment operation is not.
  2. How do you make POST retry safe? -> Client-generated idempotency key stored server-side with a unique constraint.
  3. If DELETE returns 404 on retry, is it still idempotent? -> Yes, the final state is the same; only the response differs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer recites the table. The senior links it to retry behaviour of OkHttp and gateways, and says exactly which endpoints get idempotency keys.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky-network retry on POST /payments charged users twice because the endpoint had no dedupe.

questions.promptHtml: When do you return 401 versus 403, and 400 versus 422? How should the client react to each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Status codes drive client retry logic and monitoring. Wrong codes cause real bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: 401 means I do not know who you are, so missing or expired token; the client refreshes the token and retries once. 403 means I know who you are and you are not allowed; no retry. 400 is malformed or invalid input, 422 is well-formed but violates a business rule; either is fine if the team is consistent. Neither is retried, because the same request fails the same way.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
First digit: 2xx ok, 4xx client fault, 5xx server fault. The retry rule falls out of that: 4xx (except 408 and 429) must not be retried, 5xx and 429 may be retried with exponential backoff and jitter.

401 + WWW-Authenticate  -> refresh token, retry once
403                     -> show "no access", never retry
400/422 + field errors  -> show validation, never retry
429 + Retry-After       -> wait, then retry
503                     -> retry with jitter

A private resource you should not reveal can return 404 instead of 403 (GitHub does this) to avoid leaking existence.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• 200 with {"error":...}: breaks caches, monitoring and client logic.
  • 500 for validation errors: pollutes the error-rate alert.
  • 404 for an empty list; it should be 200 [].

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Expired token on a user who is allowed? -> 401, not 403.
  2. Why 404 sometimes instead of 403? -> Avoid confirming that a private resource exists.
  3. Which 4xx may be retried? -> 408 and 429, with backoff.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior lists meanings. Senior ties each code to client behaviour and to the dashboards: 4xx rate vs 5xx rate must mean different things.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A client retried 400s in a loop after an app release sent a bad field, tripling load for hours.

questions.promptHtml: How do you design URLs for an order that can be cancelled, refunded and re-delivered, without putting verbs everywhere? How deep should nesting go?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can model actions as resources and reason about long-term URL commitments.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: URLs are plural nouns, the method is the verb. For actions that are not CRUD I model the action as a resource: POST /orders/42/cancellation or POST /payments/99/refunds, which creates a refund. Google's POST /orders/42:cancel is an acceptable escape hatch; I pick one style and keep it. I nest at most two levels, because once a thing has a global id, /orders/42 is enough.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
GET    /users/7/orders?status=PAID&limit=20   ownership in path, filters in query
POST   /orders                                create
POST   /orders/42/cancellation                action as noun (creates a cancellation record)
POST   /payments/99/refunds                   each refund has its own id, status, amount

Modelling the action as a resource gives you history, status, idempotency and partial refunds for free. Ids: use opaque UUID or ULID if enumeration leaks business volume (sequential ids say "we have 1.2M orders"). Lowercase, hyphens, no trailing slash, no extension.

Decision gravity: URLs are a one-way door once mobile apps you cannot force to update depend on them.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• /getOrder, /cancelOrder verbs in URLs.
  • /a/1/b/2/c/3/d/4 deep nesting that breaks when parentage changes.
  • Mixing /user/7 and /orders.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cancel is idempotent; which method? -> POST to the cancellation resource, return the existing one on repeat, or PUT /orders/42/cancellation.
  2. How to filter? -> Query parameters, never path segments.
  3. When is a :verb style better? -> When the action has no useful resource to model, like :start on a VM.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives CRUD only. Senior models the action, names the one-way-door cost and the id-leak issue.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team renamed /user/7/order URLs; 2-year-old app versions kept calling the old route and needed a permanent redirect layer.

questions.contextHtml:
The Orders API wraps every response so the Android team has one parser. Controller snippet and the on-call dashboard:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@PostMapping("/orders")
public ResponseEntity<?> create(@RequestBody OrderReq r) {
    try {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(service.create(r));
    } catch (ValidationException e) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of("error", e.getMessage()));
    } catch (Exception e) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of("error", "failed: " + e));
    }
}
@PostMapping("/orders")
fun create(@RequestBody r: OrderReq): ResponseEntity<Any> = try {
    ResponseEntity.ok(service.create(r))
} catch (e: ValidationException) {
    ResponseEntity.ok(mapOf("error" to e.message))
} catch (e: Exception) {
    ResponseEntity.ok(mapOf("error" to "failed: $e"))
}
orders-api  5xx rate: 0.0%   p99: 180ms   status=200: 100%
support tickets "order not created": 340 this week
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, it handles exceptions." It misses that the dashboard cannot see failures, and that e.toString() leaks internals.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do clients branch on the error string today? Are there old app versions depending on 200? Does the gateway cache POST? Who consumes the dashboard?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add an alert on a business metric (orders created per minute) because the HTTP error rate is blind.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 340 tickets come from silent failures hidden behind 200. Second, validation issues are real user errors counted as success. Third, the Exception branch hides outages.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log count of branches taken per minute, grep logs for failed:, compare orders table inserts vs POST count.
  5. Root cause: Every outcome returns 200, so caches, load balancers, retries and SLO dashboards all see success. A stack trace string also leaks internals.
  6. Fix: Map validation to 422 (or 400), unexpected to 500 with a generic body, both as application/problem+json with a code and request_id. Use a single @ControllerAdvice instead of try/catch per method. Ship behind the new API version for old apps that parse 200 bodies.
  7. Prevention: Contract test asserting status codes per error case; alert on 4xx and 5xx separately.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep 200 "for one simple parser"; Retrofit already exposes errorBody().

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old apps parse the 200 body -> Keep the old shape under /v1, new codes under /v2, measure usage.
  • Should validation be 400 or 422? -> Either, be consistent and document it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team saw a flat 0% error rate during a database outage because every handler caught and returned 200. Customer support found the outage before monitoring did.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sees nothing wrong.
  • Hire: proper 4xx/5xx and no leaked message.
  • Strong hire: adds central error mapper, problem+json, migration plan for old clients and alert strategy.

questions.contextHtml:
A security review of the ride-history API flags the endpoint below. 400K DAU, JWT auth, ids are sequential bigints.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@GetMapping("/rides/{id}")
public Ride get(@PathVariable long id, @AuthenticationPrincipal User u) {
    return rideRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow(NotFound::new);
}

@PutMapping("/users/me")
public User update(@RequestBody User body) {
    return userRepo.save(body);   // body bound straight to entity
}
@GetMapping("/rides/{id}")
fun get(@PathVariable id: Long, @AuthenticationPrincipal u: User): Ride =
    rideRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow { NotFound() }

@PutMapping("/users/me")
fun update(@RequestBody body: User): User = userRepo.save(body)
GET /rides/100234  -> 200 (my ride)
GET /rides/100235  -> 200 (someone else's ride, with pickup address)
questions.promptHtml: What are the vulnerabilities and how do you fix them?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add HTTPS and JWT expiry." The login is fine; the bug is missing authorization on the object.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this public, how long was it live, do access logs show enumeration, is PII involved (regulatory notice)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the ownership check and rate-limit the endpoint; check logs for sequential id scans.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: BOLA/IDOR on /rides/{id} (OWASP API #1). Mass assignment on PUT /users/me: client can send "role":"admin". Third, sequential ids make enumeration trivial.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the call with user B's token against user A's ride; send {"role":"ADMIN"} to the update endpoint in staging; query logs for ascending id patterns from one token.
  5. Root cause: The code checks "logged in", never "is this object mine".
  6. Fix: rideRepo.findByIdAndUserId(id, u.id), returning 404 (not 403) when not owned. Bind requests to a DTO with allow-listed fields (name, city). Move to ULIDs as defence in depth, not as the fix.
  7. Prevention: Authorization tests per endpoint (user B cannot read user A), central policy layer, API security scan in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely on obscure ids as the only control, and I would not do checks only in the UI.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Admin endpoints need to read any ride -> Separate role-checked route, audit logged.
  • 404 vs 403? -> 404 avoids confirming existence.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A telecom-style leak came from an endpoint that was authenticated but never authorized; the tokens were valid, the crypto fine.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: talks only about TLS.
  • Hire: finds IDOR and fixes with ownership query.
  • Strong hire: also finds mass assignment, tests, logs review and notification duty.

questions.contextHtml:
Product says: "Add a Download my statement button; it is sometimes slow." Backend today builds a PDF inline in GET /statements?month=.... 20K exports/day, p50 3 s, p99 70 s. The load balancer idle timeout is 60 s and you see this:

GET /statements  504  upstream timed out (60s)   count=410 last hour
questions.promptHtml: How do you design this, and what do you ask before you start?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise the load balancer timeout to 120 s." That ties up connections and threads and the next slowdown breaks it again.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Max size and format? Must the user wait on screen or can they get a push/email? Is the same statement requested repeatedly (cacheable)? Is it sensitive, so download links must expire? What is the real p99 driver (data volume, one slow query)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache generated PDFs by (user, month) and add a query timeout so a runaway job cannot hold a worker.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Synchronous generation holds a connection for the full job. Large accounts drive the p99 tail. A missing index on the statement query makes it worse.
  4. How I'd verify each: Histogram of duration by account size, EXPLAIN on the statement query, thread-pool saturation metric.
  5. Root cause: Work that can exceed the gateway timeout is done in the request path.
  6. Fix: Async job. POST /statement-exports {month} returns 202 Accepted with Location: /statement-exports/77. Client polls GET /statement-exports/77 (status queued, running, done, failed) or gets a push notification; when done it contains a short-lived signed URL. POST takes an idempotency key so a double tap makes one job.
  7. Prevention: Per-user concurrency cap, TTL on files, alert on queue age.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Polling costs requests (poll with backoff, or push); I would not open a long-lived connection for a minutes-long job.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 100x more users -> Queue with worker autoscaling and a per-user cap.
  • Webhook instead of polling? -> For server clients yes; on mobile prefer push plus a poll fallback.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "just raise the timeout" change on a report endpoint kept a thread pool full during a month-end spike and took the whole API down.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases timeouts.
  • Hire: 202 plus job resource and polling.
  • Strong hire: clarifies requirements first, adds idempotency, signed expiring URLs, caps and observability.

questions.promptHtml: How would you design the error format for a public API used by Android, iOS and web clients?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Error design shows API maturity: stable contracts, supportability and security awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One shape for every error, following RFC 9457 problem details: type, title, status, detail, plus a stable machine-readable code, a request_id, and field-level errors[] for validation. Clients switch on code, never on message text. Return all field errors in one response and never leak stack traces or SQL.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/insufficient-funds",
  "title": "Insufficient funds",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Balance 120.00 is less than the 250.00 requested.",
  "code": "INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS",
  "request_id": "req_8f3a1c",
  "errors": [{ "field": "amount", "message": "must be <= balance" }]
}

The request_id ties the user's complaint to the exact log line. The code is a contract, so renaming it is a breaking change just like renaming a field. Every service behind the gateway must map to this one shape. Auth errors need care: "no such user" vs "wrong password" enables account enumeration.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
record ApiError(String code, String detail, String requestId) {}
// Spring Boot 3: ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, "...");
data class ApiError(val code: String, val detail: String?, val request_id: String?)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Free-text-only errors that force string matching.
  • Different shapes per microservice leaking through the gateway.
  • Stack traces in 500 bodies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Localised messages? -> Client localises by code; detail is for developers and logs.
  2. One error or all? -> All field errors at once, saving round trips.
  3. How do you evolve codes? -> Add new codes only; clients treat unknown codes by status class.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE returns a message string. Senior adds stable codes, trace ids, one gateway-wide mapper and security hygiene.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Support could not locate failures until errors carried a request id searchable in logs.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments dashboard (web, JavaScript) and the Android app show wrong numbers for some customers. Sample response and complaints:

{ "id": 9007199254740993, "amount": 19.99, "created": 1731146130,
  "status": "PAID", "items": [ { "price": 0.1 }, { "price": 0.2 } ] }
Web: id shows 9007199254740992 (off by one) -> refund API returns 404
Android: total shows 0.30000000000000004 on receipt
Another dev: "created" is seconds in one service and millis in another
iOS crash: new status "PARTIALLY_REFUNDED" -> exhaustive enum switch
questions.promptHtml: List what is wrong with this contract and how you fix it without breaking shipped apps.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Round on the client." That hides symptoms and leaves the 64-bit id broken.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which app versions are live and what share? Are amounts stored as decimals or floats in the DB? Can we add fields without clients crashing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a string id (id_str) and a decimal-safe amount alongside the old fields.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 64-bit id above 2^53 loses precision in JS. Floating-point money. Ambiguous time unit. Closed enum handling in the client.
  4. How I'd verify each: Number(9007199254740993) in a console; check DB column type; grep services for System.currentTimeMillis() vs seconds; check client enum parsing.
  5. Root cause: The contract uses types the consumers cannot represent exactly, with no unit or tolerance rules.
  6. Fix: ids as strings, money as integer minor units plus currency ("amount_minor":1999,"currency":"INR"), dates ISO 8601 UTC ("2026-11-09T10:15:30Z"), enums as strings with an UNKNOWN fallback and clients told to tolerate unknown values.
  7. Prevention: OpenAPI with oasdiff in CI, contract tests, a style guide.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not change fields in place (old apps break); expand, migrate, contract. Decimal strings are fine too, floats never.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Currency with 0 or 3 decimals (JPY, KWD)? -> Minor unit exponent comes from currency, not hard-coded 2.
  • Bare array responses? -> Wrap as {data, next_cursor} before pagination is needed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A snowflake-style id above 2^53 silently mapped two orders to one in a web admin tool until ids became strings.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rounds client-side.
  • Hire: strings for ids, integer money, ISO dates.
  • Strong hire: adds additive migration, tolerant readers and CI diff checks.

questions.contextHtml:
An admin console lets support staff edit a customer profile. Two agents opened Priya's record; agent A changed the address, agent B changed the phone and saved afterwards. The address edit vanished. 60 edits/s peak, PUT /customers/{id} replaces the whole object, no concurrency control. Customer complaint volume: 25 per day, "my update disappeared".

10:02:11 A GET  /customers/7  -> {addr:"Old", phone:"111"}
10:02:15 B GET  /customers/7  -> {addr:"Old", phone:"111"}
10:03:01 A PUT  /customers/7  {addr:"New", phone:"111"}  200
10:03:40 B PUT  /customers/7  {addr:"Old", phone:"222"}  200   <- overwrites A
questions.promptHtml: Why did this happen and how do you prevent it at the API level?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use PATCH." That helps here but still loses concurrent edits of the same field and does not detect conflicts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How common is concurrent editing? Is last-write-wins acceptable for any field? Do clients re-fetch before editing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add an audit log of before/after so lost data can be recovered.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Lost update from whole-resource PUT with no precondition. Stale client form. Less likely: server bug, since both writes returned 200 as designed.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the timeline in a test; look at audit table timestamps.
  5. Root cause: Read-modify-write across two HTTP calls with no version check.
  6. Fix: Return ETag: "v17" on GET; require If-Match: "v17" on PUT. A mismatch returns 412 Precondition Failed (or 428 Precondition Required if the header is missing); UI reloads and shows a merge dialog. DB side: UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id=? AND version=?.
  7. Prevention: Make If-Match mandatory on mutable resources, test two concurrent writers, metric on 412 rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use pessimistic locks across HTTP calls (a closed browser tab keeps the lock). PATCH on disjoint fields is a good complement.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mobile client offline for hours -> Conflict resolution policy per field, or server-side merge.
  • 409 vs 412? -> 412 for a failed precondition header, 409 for a general state conflict.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A CRM silently dropped edits for months; adding version checks surfaced a 3% conflict rate nobody had known about.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames users.
  • Hire: ETag/If-Match with 412.
  • Strong hire: includes DB version check, UX for conflict, 428 and metrics.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. Release 5.8 of the Android app sent quantity: "two" (string) due to a form bug. The API returned 500 because a parse exception was uncaught. The app retried 5xx up to 5 times without backoff. 300K devices on 5.8, 40% hit the form.

12:00  POST /orders 500   rate 800/s   (baseline 600/s total)
12:05  POST /orders 500   rate 6,200/s
12:08  p99 for all endpoints 9s, DB pool exhausted, healthy endpoints 503
12:20  rolled back server, client unaffected, still retrying
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong at each layer and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale up the servers." Retried bad requests produce amplified load that never succeeds.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the app retry 4xx too? Is there a server-controlled kill switch or remote config? Did the gateway rate limit per client?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Return 429/503 with Retry-After at the gateway for this endpoint and app version, or shed that traffic; use remote config to disable the retry or ship a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Wrong status (500 instead of 400) classed as retryable. Missing backoff and jitter caused a retry storm. Shared DB pool let one endpoint starve others.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group by app version header and status; compare request rate to unique devices; pool metrics per endpoint.
  5. Root cause: A client bug turned into a server outage because validation failure was reported as 5xx, which tells clients to retry, with no backoff.
  6. Fix: Server: malformed body is 400 with problem+json, handled in a central exception mapper. Client: retry only 5xx/429/network, capped at 3 with exponential backoff plus jitter, honour Retry-After. Platform: per-endpoint bulkheads and per-client rate limits.
  7. Prevention: Fuzz/contract tests on request types, alert on 5xx caused by parse errors, canary rollout of app releases.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not simply stop all retries; they are valuable for real 503s.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retried POST creates duplicates? -> Idempotency key on the order call.
  • How do you block 5.8 only? -> Gateway rule on X-App-Version returning 426 or a soft block.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single mistyped field in a mobile release produced a self-inflicted DDoS of 10x baseline because every layer treated failure as transient.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale up.
  • Hire: 400 vs 500 and backoff.
  • Strong hire: layered fix with jitter, Retry-After, bulkheads, version-based shedding and review actions.

questions.contextHtml: Your public API uses /getUserOrders?id=7 and returns a bare array of orders with price in float rupees. You want /users/7/orders returning {data, next_cursor} with amount_minor ints. Traffic: 40M requests/day, 6 mobile app versions live; versions older than 2 years are 8% of calls, plus 30 partner integrations you cannot force to move.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate without breaking anyone, and what is the decision gravity?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Ship v2 and tell everyone." Ignores that old apps cannot be updated and no usage data exists.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we have per-client-version traffic metrics? Can we contact partners? Is there a business deadline (security, cost)? Is a force-upgrade gate available in the app?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; add telemetry first (app version, partner key, endpoint) and a Deprecation plan.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Expand-contract can finish in a few months if partners respond; the long tail (old apps) decides the end date; bare-array to envelope is the riskiest change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Dashboards by client version, traffic per partner; shadow-compare old and new responses.
  5. Root cause: URL and shape are public commitments; this is a one-way door for external clients.
  6. Fix: Add /v2/users/{id}/orders implemented on the same core service with thin adapters. Keep /getUserOrders working, add Deprecation: true and Sunset: <date> headers, ship both fields (price, amount_minor) during the overlap. Notify partners with a changelog and dates.
  7. Prevention: oasdiff in CI, style guide for new endpoints, versioning from day one.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove the old route until traffic is below an agreed threshold (for example under 1%), and then a final gate (426 or min-supported-version screen) for the tail. I would not copy the whole code base into a v2 fork.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Security hole in the old route -> Fix in both, and escalate the sunset.
  • Partner refuses to migrate -> Contract/commercial decision; keep a frozen adapter with cost owner.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company kept a "temporary" v1 for six years because nobody had telemetry on who was still calling it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: breaking cutover.
  • Hire: new version plus deprecation window.
  • Strong hire: telemetry-driven sunset, shared core with adapters, partner comms and force-upgrade as last resort.

questions.contextHtml:
The feed endpoint returns 20 items, 2 KB JSON each (40 KB per page) to Android users, most on 1 Mbps 3G in your target market. 5M DAU, each opens the feed 6 times a day. egress cost is about 0.08 USD/GB (verify your own price). Median screen time-to-content is 1.4 s; 60% of requests re-fetch data that has not changed. Only 600 bytes per item are shown on screen.

GET /feed?limit=20   200  40,000 B  (no Content-Encoding, no ETag)
questions.promptHtml: Estimate savings and propose changes in order of effort.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to gRPC." Large rewrite; compression, field selection and conditional GET give most of the gain for little effort.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which fields are really used? Are responses personalised (affects CDN caching)? What is the p95 device and network?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn on Accept-Encoding: gzip (or brotli): JSON shrinks 70 to 90%, 40 KB becomes about 6 KB.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Compression is the largest quick win. Field trimming is next. Conditional GET removes the 60% of unchanged re-fetches. Protocol change is the least cost-effective.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure bytes on the wire and TTFB per change in a staged rollout; compare p50/p95 time to content.
  5. Root cause: Over-fetching and no cache validators.
  6. Fix and math: Daily requests = 5M x 6 = 30M. Before: 30M x 40 KB = 1.2 TB/day. gzip to 6 KB: 180 GB. Add ?fields= trimming to 600 B per item (12 KB raw, about 2.5 KB gzipped): 75 GB. With ETag and 304 on 60% of calls (about 200 B each): 12M x 2.5 KB + 18M x 0.2 KB = 33.6 GB/day. About 97% less. At 0.08 USD/GB that is about 96 USD to 2.7 USD per day, and on 1 Mbps the transfer goes from 0.32 s to about 0.02 s.
  7. Prevention: Payload budget in CI, size dashboards per endpoint.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: ETag generation costs CPU or a version lookup; personalised feeds are not CDN-cacheable; I would not support arbitrary fields= without allow-listing (it can become a query-cost hole).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Feed changes every few seconds -> ETag hit rate falls; use cursor + since delta instead.
  • Does GraphQL help? -> Solves field selection but loses HTTP caching; use only if many client shapes exist.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Enabling compression and a 304 path on one chatty endpoint cut mobile data usage by an order of magnitude and improved app ratings in low-bandwidth regions.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rewrite in a new protocol.
  • Hire: gzip, field trimming, ETag.
  • Strong hire: shows math, ordering by effort, caveats on personalisation and caching.
